item: Row 335: a recorded header descriptor is checked to still be ours before it is reused or closed
summary: The parked header descriptors (R789) were trusted by number. If another part of the process closed one of them, SQLite or another file could get the same number, and the sweep then closed it as ours, dropping the store's fcntl lock, or a read went through it to the wrong file. Every reuse and close now checks, under the header lock, that the number still leads to the recorded file (fstat dev and inode) and was opened our way (read-only, O_NONBLOCK, no O_NOFOLLOW). A failed or erroring check never reads or closes: the record is forgotten and the store counts as held, so the sweep fails closed, including for a record forgotten while it was listing. is_encrypted_file re-checks the file after its read. Five deterministic tests reuse a freed number (read-write and read-only connections, another file, another store, mid-sweep), and a sixth pins the header read's re-check; mutation: dropping the (device, inode) half, the whole flags half, the sweep's validation or the forgotten list each fails a test (SQLite's descriptors differ in both O_NONBLOCK and O_NOFOLLOW, so either flag alone suffices). A header read answers only from the file the name leads to; three reads that land elsewhere answer as an unreadable file always has (None), never a verdict from another file's bytes. Limits stated in the code: a number reused while a reader is using it, a fstat under the lock on a hung mount, a passing fstat error leaving a descriptor open (the ruling forgets, never closes), and macOS not reporting O_NOFOLLOW.
